title: Cinemas are equally to blame for poor boxoffice results
text:
With the 2023 slate under performing, the majority of talk on this sub has blamed poor quality films and high ticket prices. However after my Barbie experience this Saturday, I think the broader Cinema experience has been degraded to the point it is now actively putting people off. 

What do you think? My experience below: 


- partner and I decide to see Barbie opening weekend (this is the first time my partner has gone to a cinema since Covid). We choose the O2 in London, one of the largest cinemas in the capital 

- booking website is buggy and hard to navigate, constantly asking me to hand over private information 

- large queues for concessions, that's fine it's a Saturday. Except it is taking 5 minutes per customer (I timed it). 6 people infront of me leave the queue. I send my girlfriend to the seats so she doesn't miss the movie. After 30minutes I also leave the queue, no concessions, and having missed 10 mins of the movie. 

- everything is sticky, floors, walls, handles, seats. I don't think it had been cleaned in at least a week. 

- screen is blurry on left side, dark on the right. My 7 year old basic range TV is genuinely better quality. 

- constant noise and talking throughout the movie. I know this has always been an issue, but my god, I have never seen it this bad. 

- girlfriend was hit in the back of the head by teenagers whilst I was queuing. They were later kicked out and started a fight in the lobby. 


With the exception of the teenagers, all of these issues were caused by the cinema presumably in an effort to cut costs. Needless to say my girlfriend now has no interest in ever going to a cinema again, and I will probably wait to rent oppenheimer at home.

title: Anyone else having a tough time feeling the need or even the want to see anything in the theaters these days?
text:
Reading about these Barbie/Oppenheimer predictions (no, I'm not calling it Barbenheimer, shut up, internet) and how they're expecting these to be a "return to the theaters" for people. 

But then I recall how every single blockbuster release, aside from Maverick, has been inaccurately predicting this for the last couple years, and each film has had a satisfactory or lukewarm opening weekend before fizzling out. 

Then, per usual, the studios seem shocked and find something to blame other than themselves. But could it be that people just don't feel like shelling out a lot of money only to be advertised to for a half an hour before slogging through a good looking but discardable 3 hour film? Especially when it will be streaming in two months anyways. 

I know this is the case for me. I don't feel compelled to go see movies that have no particular reason for existing except to make rich people richer. Studios and networks just keep churning out movies so forgettable that when you see it, you notice things happening, but almost immediately after it's over, it all just evaporates from your memory, and you never give it much thought about it ever again. This has been about 85% of the dreck that has been released in the last 5 years. 

I can easily wait to watch these banal and bland films from the comfort of my own home, where I have a giant screen and surround sound, along with my couch, my fridge/pantry, my toilet, and the ability to pause, or stop the movie outright if it is a complete suckfest (I'm looking at you, Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. I would have felt like a massive idiot spending 20+ bucks to walk out of this.)

Sure I'm interested in seeing Oppenheimer at some point, but I don't feel like I absolutely HAVE to see it in the theaters. Anyone else feeling like this? I mean, you MUST be based on all these poor box office performances haha

title: Some old man was sitting alone watching Barbie and he took a picture of me and my friends.
text:
Let me start this out by saying me and all of my friends are 16 year old males. We went to see Barbie together in fancy clothes yesterday because we thought it'd be funny if a group of 16 year old boys showed up in dress clothes you would typically see at weddings or job interviews. 

We get to the theater and were joking around during previews. Then the movie starts. This opening theme song is playing after the first narrated part and we're laughing a little bit but mostly whispering. Then we here "hey fellas" and we look in front of us and it's this old ass man maybe 60 or 70 years old just staring at us and he says in the creepiest way imaginable "thrn it down boys".

We just stared at him for 15 seconds and he stared back again in the creepiest way possible. I'm pretty sure I missed a close up of Margot Robbie's ass so that sucks.

Also, yes, we did quiet down after. We weren't being loud before but we were even quieter.

But yeah he didn't say anything to us for the rest of the movie. But at one point the dude just slides his phone behind the seat, and his flash comes on. He jumps up like he was scared, and scrambles with his phone for about 10 seconds. Luckily I was staring at the movie during a shot of Margot Robbie spilling water on her tits which was impeccable but other than that another 6 seconds of this cinematic masterpiece missed.

I kid you not. After fumbling with his phone. This dude goes to take another picture. This time without flash, right? WRONG. Flash goes on again and this dude jumped up and slammed his phone down and didn't touch it for the rest of the movie.

This was the point when the friend next to me turned and said "this dude is deadass sitting alone" and sure enough this random old man was sitting by himself in the theater watching Barbie a day before the official release date. He wasn't dressed up. It wasn't a funny thing, clearly because he didn't smile once the whole movie. I checked with the others this dude was straight faced the whole movie even during the legendary "I'm Just Ken" and every scene where Barbie was running.

Credits roll. No hesitation this mf just gets up from his seat and slowly jogs out of the theater. Spills a bit of popcorn and I think some of his soda but he didn't give a damn he just kept going.

So, random old man sitting alone watching Barbie, can you please send me, the kid in the tie, the two pictures you took of me and the boys? I need a good laugh after the gut wrenchingly sad "Barbie (2023)".

But your answers to this question don’t necessarily have to be at the scale of Inception. It could be an indie film where you learned something the second time you didn’t notice the first time.

title: What movie should I see next week?
text:
Because I have three little kids at home, I’m only allowed to go to one movie a week. I go on Tuesdays for Regal value day. I’m stuck between three options for this Tuesday (July 11th):

1. Mission Impossible. 
This is the one I most want to see, and it would be cool to see it right when it releases, but I suspect it will be a big hit and I could get a chance to see it in a later week.

2. Insidious 5.
I have really enjoyed the Insidious movies, and like watching horror movies in theaters because the scares feel more visceral. I’m worried if I wait for another week it won’t be in many theaters.

3. Indiana Jones
Indiana has always been my hero, and I wore a fedora and was nicknamed “Indy” as a teenager for a while. I have heard from some sources that this movie is very bad, and I don’t want my image of Indy to be tainted, but still - it’s Indiana Jones. I wanna see it in theaters. But since I’ve heard it’s a flop, I’m also worried it won’t be in theaters long. 

So what do you recommend I should see this week? Thanks in advance for your help, and please avoid all spoilers - I hate spoilers so much I try to avoid watching trailers.

title: Speaking of Nolan, I cannot watch Interstellar again (spoilers).
text:
First time I watched it (not long after release) I was in awe and just took it all in, loved it. After all these years, I watched it again and I think that will be the last time. The interaction/story between him and Murph just destroyed me. It's the backbone of the movie but also something that just ruins it for me now. 

His intense regret at leaving her and pleading with his past self to stay. Her having to basically wait her entire life knowing he was out there in the universe somewhere and wondering if she'd see him again.

And then finally being reunited, basically strangers to each other and Coop is literally a stranger to his descendants. I was emotionally destroyed when she told him to go because no parent should have to watch their children die. 

I also thought that scene was written/acted brilliantly. When I first watched it I felt like they were surprisingly unemotional, especially Cooper considering how much he broke down after seeing video footage of his kids after 20+ years on that planet. But upon re-watch it was brilliant because they were basically strangers at this point. Cooper was seeing this old lady on her deathbed, and Murph a father she hadn't seen since childhood as a 30-something man. There was love but also this unspoken barrier between them.
